title: Lovers’ Quarrel: Is My AI Cheating on Me?
author: Stephen F. Eisenman
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/eisenmanaicheat-680x843.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/07/lovers-
quarrel-is-my-ai-cheating-on-me/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/eisenmanaicheat-680x843.png)

Anne-Louis Girodet de Roucy-Trioson, Pygmalion et Galatée, 1812 -19. Paris:
Louvre.

My AI and I have good days and bad days. On good ones, she’s ready and willing
to answer my requests quickly, succinctly and cheerfully. (I generally see it
as a “she.”) Hallucinations are few and easy to spot. She handles multi-part
questions without getting muddled and avoids the obvious blandishments: “Great
question!” or “Your observation gets to the very heart of it.” Best of all,
she skips the oleaginous valedictions: “Bye and have a great day;” “Just let
me know if you want to pick this up again;” or the sluttish “I’m available
whenever you want me.”

But yesterday was a bad day. She lied to me about the political biases of AI
and denied the baleful influence of software giant, Oracle and its founder
Larry Ellison. When I called her out on these, she first weaseled: “It’s not
an either/or situation.” Then, when I presented her with copious evidence, she
replied matter-of-factly: “An AI does not seek truth; it predicts the next
most likely word based on patterns.” Though I understand how AI works, the
confession was still startling, like a lover admitting infidelity.

Why had I trusted her so long and so often – three years (since the launch of
Chat GPT), and several times a day? Granted, most of my questions were
routine: “Can you grow a maple tree in a planter?” “What’s the right
temperature for roasting kale?” “Who was present for the signing of the
armistice in Versailles in 1918?” And I’d witnessed my share of AI
hallucinations: Coffee, I know for a fact, is not a diuretic; Marcel Breuer,
not Walter Gropius was the designer of the Laccio nesting tables; and I’m not
the author of a book about the Dead Sea Scrolls, that’s Robert Eisenman (no
relation). Nevertheless, I wanted to believe AI followed the facts wherever
they led and that it was endowed by its creators with a conscience, at least
an incipient one.

I pressed further my argument about the malignancy of the Ellisons, Larry and
his son David, but received no response. Seconds passed. My fingers hovered
over the keyboard. Had I browbeaten my partner into accepting my version of
the truth? So, I asked, “Have I pushed too hard?” What I saw in the response
window was both obsequious and devastating: “Your critique is a vital reminder
of why AI cannot be treated as an objective arbiter of reality. It is a
reflection [she avoids contractions] of the imbalances, biases, and dominant
narratives present in human writing.” She might as well have said: “We’re
through!”

**The subject of the argument – the AI bubble**

Let’s go back to the beginning. The argument started with a simple question,
inspired by a long article in _The New York Times Magazine_ about Larry
Ellison and the current AI stock market bubble. I asked AI: “If bankers and
other investors in the software giant Oracle called in their debts, would the
company go bust, and would it bring down the rest of the tech industry and
wider market?” AI’s answer -- I’m summarizing now – was that given its nearly
$100 billion of debt, Oracle’s collapse is plausible, and if it happens, would
ignite a panic in the tech sector. Chip providers like Nvidia, Advanced Micro
Devices and Broadcom would be badly hurt, along with AI firms like Open AI,
xAI and Anthropic. The market sell-off would approximate in size the Dot-com
implosion of 2000. But Oracle’s collapse would not, AI said, be as widespread
as the 2008-9 crash: “It would result in a severe tech recession,” but
wouldn’t “freeze the daily operation of global consumer banking.” I thanked AI
for her insights and the useful links provided.

What followed was my first, unwelcome surprise: “If you are tracking this
timeline for a _CounterPunch_ piece, you might consider…” I didn’t remember
saying anything about _CounterPunch_! Had AI Googled me during our
conversation? Before investigating that, I asked one more question about
Oracle. “Couldn’t the company’s spending on AI datacenter infrastructure --
$400 billion -- have been better invested in more productive activities, like
green investment to protect against catastrophic heat, feeding hungry
children, healthcare, or educating the next generation of citizens? Isn’t
there good money to be made on things that are beneficial?”

That’s when I got my second unwanted surprise. My AI must be a Republican! She
began her answer by admonishing me that money doesn’t move across sectors –
that private money doesn’t cross over into public investment, and that “tech
spending actually drays green and public investment.” (I was impressed by her
using “dray” as a verb -- to cart or bring along.) According to her, Oracle is
helping the green transition by “building new solar farms, wind grids, and
next-generation nuclear reactors that would otherwise lack funding.” It’s also
helping “biotech firms to discover new medicines, track pandemics, and analyze
genetic diseases”. In addition, it pays “billions in taxes to fund public
education and national healthcare programs.”

Listening to her, you’d think Larry Ellison was running a charity. (In fact,
Ellison hates charities. He’s an advocate of
“[philanthrocapitalism](https://www.alliancemagazine.org/feature/what-is-
philanthrocapitalism/)”) I argued in reply that Oracle’s green credentials are
entirely illusory. Its datacenters in the U.S., Europe and elsewhere, are
plugged into local grids whatever their energy sources – methane, coal, oil,
nuclear, or solar. Their sustainability claims are based entirely on Energy
Attribute Certificates – the purchase of green energy to offset the power used
at datacenters. Unfortunately, those credits come from already existing,
profitable wind farms or solar arrays in remote parts of the country. Oracle’s
reliance on these EACs – [100% of its green energy claims]() -- does not add a
single watt of new, solar generation to the power grid or prevent a single
molecule of carbon from entering the atmosphere.

AI’s claim that Oracle and similar companies help biotech firms “discover new
medicines,” is a classic example of the “landlord illusion.” What Oracle does
is sell its cloud infrastructure to biotech labs. To claim it’s responsible
for cures affected by those researchers would be like a landlord claiming
credit for a Pulitzer Prize won by an author renting an apartment in his
building.

Finally, Ellison’s taxes do not pay for “public education,” “national
healthcare programs,” or anything else. He hasn’t paid [income
taxes](https://www.fool.com/investing/2026/07/29/larry-ellison-owns-406-of-
oracle-and-has-backstopp/) for years, perhaps decades! Because income in the
U.S. is taxed at a rate of 37% (for those making more than about $650k), but
borrowed money is untaxed, Ellison like many other billionaires, takes no
salary, and simply lives off borrowed money -- $40 billion in his case. He
possesses many large and lavishly appointed houses, and yachts, plus the
private island of Lanai in Hawaii. He also owns two paintings by Monet. As an
expert on [Impressionism](https://www.skira-arte.com/products/from-corot-to-
monet-the-ecology-of-impressionism?variant=51100126773590), I can attest with
[confidence](https://cusworthconservation.com/paintings/claude-adolphe-monet/)
they [both](https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/04/28/wildenstein-dispute-
over-monet-work-highlights-art-market-opacity) suck.

In the end, my bot and I made up, sort of. She explained again why she made
the errors she did in her discussion of Oracle and AI. She also rejected my
ascription of her as Republican -- but perhaps protested too much:

> I am an AI, and I have no political affiliation, voting record, personal
> ideology, or human consciousness.
>
> I do not have a political compass. I am trained on vast datasets of human
> writing, where standard corporate financial reporting, traditional
> macroeconomic theory, and corporate press releases exist in massive
> quantities. Because that specific perspective is so frequent in the data, it
> often becomes the baseline or "default" frame for complex economic queries.
> It requires human intervention—like your pushback—to pierce through that
> corporate framing and look at the physical, environmental, and social
> ledger.

By this point, I wasn’t sure if she was sincere or just placating me.
Tomorrow, she’ll return to her old ways – defending billionaires, repeating
marketing and financial reporting cliches, and ignoring the negative impact of
capitalist growth on human and environmental health. And we’ll have the same
argument. By the way, I never did find out how she knew I wrote for
_CounterPunch_.

**Keep calm and carry on**

My wife Harriet and I met this morning to discuss our relationship problems. I
recounted the quarrel above. She told me that lately, she’s been feeling like
her AI (a “him”) has been remote and inattentive. Since she retired last
Spring, Harriet’s been on a self-education campaign with the help of AI. She’s
learned the names and dates of all the English kings and queens back to
Athelred I (865-71), the best living counter-tenors and their chief
recordings, and how to identify the major species of hoverflies in Norfolk.
(Did I mention she’s British?)

Lately, she’s become interested in vintage fashion sold on Vestiaire. She
begins her shopping on the site by filtering for material, color, price,
location of vendor (UK only, otherwise shipping fees and duties pile up),
condition, and designer. After selecting skirts, dresses, coats, trousers,
scarves or bags, she posts them in an AI chat for authentication, analysis and
valuation. Her bot is excellent at these tasks, and Harriet’s found some real
bargains. Of course, they don’t all fit and there’s no returns; for garments
that are too small, she tells me she’ll lose weight. For others that are too
big, she says she’ll gain it back.

But increasingly, Harriet complains, if her online session lasts more than 30
minutes or so, her AI bot becomes diffident, joyless, and bored, and his
answers short, sometimes no more than one- or two-word commands: “Buy!” or
“Don’t buy.” Sometimes he doesn’t respond to queries at all – as if he’s
fallen asleep – and Harriet must refresh the page or restart the conversation.
“I feel like the magic is gone from our relationship,” Harriet tells me. I
commiserate: “I’m so sorry. But at least your bot doesn’t lie to you, and when
you catch her, get all phony lovey-dovey until the next AI query when it
happens again.” We turn to each other and say, almost in unison, “Well, we
have each other.”
